vignette:
Nadia is a 77-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who has lived alone for many years and supports herself by tutoring children and college students, usually in their homes, at the public library, or online when she can arrange it. She describes the defining trauma of her life as having been a civilian in a war zone when she was a young woman. What remains most vivid is not a broad political story but a single episode of terror in which bombardment came close enough that she believed, with complete certainty, that she would die. She remembers the sound first, then the violent force of it, people shouting, and the frantic need to get out and find a way to survive. The memory is fixed around escape and the impossibility of knowing where safety was. Even now, when she speaks about it, she does not recount it as something distant. She says that remembering it brings back the same terror she felt at the time, as if her body has never accepted that the danger ended.

In the years afterward, Nadia built a life in the United States and became known as a patient, serious tutor. She can still describe the person she believes she was before the war: more open, more emotionally alive, less vigilant, less burdened by the sense that disaster could break through ordinary life without warning. She dwells on that earlier version of herself with grief and bitterness. In her mind there is a clear dividing line between the woman she used to be and the woman who survived. She has come to believe that this change says something shameful about her. When she notices how fearful and constricted her life has become, she concludes, "I am a weak person." She does not say this dramatically; she says it as if it were a settled fact.

The memory intrudes into the present in ways that still frighten her. Something in her surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning: a sudden loud sound in the street outside a student's apartment, the echo of a slammed door in a library corridor, even the strained look on people's faces when there is confusion nearby. In those moments she does not experience herself as a woman in her seventies in a safe American city. She feels as though the event is happening right now. The panic is immediate and total. She becomes acutely aware of exits, distances, obstacles, and whether she could get out fast enough if she had to. Because of this, she has developed the habit of staying near exits wherever she goes. If she is tutoring in a family's living room, she chooses the chair closest to the door. In the library, she scans the room before settling down and prefers tables with a direct line to the exit. She does this quietly, almost automatically, but it determines where she can sit, how long she can stay, and whether she can concentrate on her students.

Over time, her life has narrowed around efforts not to be overwhelmed. She avoids television programs, films, and reading material about war, bombings, refugees, or disasters because she is certain that if she lets herself think too directly about what happened, she will not be able to handle it. News footage is especially difficult; even a brief clip can leave her shaken, feeling the old terror in full force. She changes channels quickly, leaves articles unread, and asks students or neighbors not to discuss violent world events in front of her. This has had ordinary but painful consequences. She has withdrawn from conversations that others take for granted and sometimes appears aloof or uninterested when she is actually trying to hold herself together. She describes feeling dead inside much of the time, as though her emotional life has flattened into vigilance and endurance. Students and their parents know her as dependable, but not as warm as she once imagined herself being.

The strain has become more noticeable recently as aging has made her feel less able to recover when she is startled. A recent incident during a tutoring session brought her to seek help: a sudden crash in the hallway outside the apartment where she was working made her freeze, then feel the old terror sweep through her so completely that she could barely remain in the room. She kept her eyes on the door and could not follow the student's reading. Afterward she was ashamed and preoccupied for days, thinking again about the woman she used to be and what she sees as her own weakness. Coming to treatment, Nadia says she is afraid that if she allows the memory any space, it will swallow her whole. At the same time, she is tired of arranging every room around escape and tired of feeling empty. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the past, but to remember it without being taken back into it each time.
